verses.note: The man has just heard that he will return to dust, yet he names his wife for life. Many interpreters read this as the first response of faith to the promise of verse 15, trusting that the woman's seed will come.

The line that began to call on the LORD in 4:26 continues. Nothing remarkable is said of Enosh or Kenan, and that is itself part of the chapter's teaching: God's purpose moves forward through ordinary, unrecorded faithfulness from one generation to the next.

In a chapter where every life ends in death, one ends in God's presence. The text does not explain where Enoch went, but it shows that death is not the final word for a person who walks with God. Later Scripture turns this hope into the promise of resurrection.

Lamech's hope is aimed at the curse on the ground. After the flood God promises never again to curse the ground because of man (8:21), and Noah becomes a man of the soil who plants a vineyard (9:20). Scripture's fuller answer is the removal of the curse itself (Revelation 22:3).

The chapter ends with the waters prevailing and no word from God. The silence is deliberate. The turn of the story in 8:1, "But God remembered Noah", shows that the hope of the ark never rested on the water's height but on God's faithfulness.

The verb yachal, used of Noah's waiting in verse 12, is the same verb Israel later uses for hoping in God (Psalm 130:5; Micah 7:7). Noah's patience between promise and fulfillment is the first long wait in Scripture, and the olive leaf is the first small sign that the promise is holding.

Abraham dies owning only a burial plot. The New Testament reads the gap between promise and possession as teaching the patriarchs to look for a city God builds (Hebrews 11:9-16), and Stephen notes that God gave him ‘not even a foot of ground’ during his life (Acts 7:5).

Abraham is a stranger in the land God promised him. The Old Testament later makes this the posture of all God's people, and the New Testament calls believers foreigners and exiles (1 Peter 2:11), living now in a world whose final shape is still promised.

The first piece of the promised land that Abraham legally owns is a grave. Jeremiah will later buy a field during the Babylonian siege as a sign that fields would again be bought in the land (Jeremiah 32:9-15). Both purchases are acts of hope, deeds signed in expectation of a future God has promised.

Sarah is buried in the land, not taken back to Mesopotamia. Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob will follow her into this cave (Genesis 49:29-32), and Joseph asks that his bones be carried up from Egypt (Genesis 50:25). Hebrews 11:13-16 reads their deaths as faith looking toward a better, heavenly country.

God had promised Abraham that he would go to his fathers in peace and be buried at a good old age (Genesis 15:15), and verse 8 records that promise kept almost word for word. Jesus later argues from God's being ‘the God of Abraham’ that the patriarchs live to God (Matthew 22:31-32), and Hebrews says Abraham was looking for a city whose builder is God.

God speaks of the land as given before it is possessed. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs died without receiving what was promised, having seen it from a distance, and this verse shows why they could live that way.

Rachel's tomb became a place where Israel remembered her as a mother weeping for her children. Jeremiah hears her weeping at the exile and hears God promise that her children will come back (Jeremiah 31:15-17); Matthew applies the lament to the grief at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

Being ‘gathered to his people’ is a different act from burial, which follows it, and the phrase is used even of those buried far from their fathers. Many interpreters see in it an early sign of belief in continued existence with the ancestors, which Jesus draws on when he calls God the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of the living (Matthew 22:32).

The contrast between achuzzah for Esau and sojourning for Jacob teaches what Hebrews later says of the patriarchs: they lived as foreigners in the land of promise, looking for a city with foundations (Hebrews 11:9-10).

Sheol, named here for the first time, is where Jacob expects to go in grief. The Old Testament speaks of it without the fuller hope later revealed, and the Joseph story itself will reverse Jacob's despair when he learns that the son he mourned is alive (45:26-28).

Jacob speaks of death as a descent into Sheol, the realm of the dead, and sees nothing beyond sorrow. The Old Testament's hope for what lies past the grave grows slowly, and here it is shadowed entirely by grief.

The son Jacob mourned as dead is alive, and the father's spirit is revived by the news. The New Testament does not cite this scene, but its shape, grief over a son given up for dead turned into life, is the shape Christian hope takes in the resurrection.

The promise looks past Jacob's death. He will die in Egypt, but the promise of return is fulfilled first at his burial in Canaan and then in the exodus, teaching his descendants to read their own stay in Egypt as temporary.

Jacob can face death because what he feared lost has been given back. Luke's Simeon voices the same readiness when he sees what God had promised (Luke 2:29-30), which is a thematic parallel, not a prediction.
Jacob's burial request looks to the land God promised, not to the comfort of Egypt. The carrying out of his body in chapter 50 is a small exodus that anticipates the great one.

The dying father's last concern is not his own grave but his descendants' return. Joseph will repeat the promise almost word for word at his own death (50:24), and Moses will carry Joseph's bones out of Egypt because of it (Exodus 13:19).
Jacob's last words are about a grave in the land of promise. Owning nothing in Canaan but this cave, he insists on lying there, a claim on the future that only God's promise can make good.

Being gathered to one's people happens at death, before and apart from burial, which suggests that the patriarchs understood death as joining those who had gone before rather than simple extinction. Jesus cites God as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to show that the dead live to God (Matthew 22:32).
Joseph speaks of a visitation he will not live to see. Exodus 3:16 and 4:31 use the same verb when the promise begins to be kept, and the people who hear it believe and worship.

Genesis ends without resolution. The promise of land stands, the family is fruitful, and the one who saved them lies unburied in Egypt, waiting. The book leaves its reader waiting too, for the God who visits.

The patriarchs died without receiving the land; the promise passes to their descendants intact. Hebrews reads their waiting as faith that looked for a better country (Hebrews 11:13-16), so the land promise becomes a pattern of hope that reaches past Canaan.

God's vigil on the first Passover night becomes Israel's vigil in every later year, and later Jewish tradition read it as a night of waiting for final redemption. The verse makes remembrance of past rescue into watchfulness for the next.
David asks for a blessing that reaches beyond his life, ‘forever’. The prayer hands the future of his house to God, a hope Israel kept praying after the dynasty fell (Psalm 89:49-51).
The last word of the psalm is ‘forever’. The joy it describes is the presence of God himself, the same good confessed in verse 2, now enjoyed without end.

If the dust-bound worship God, then death does not set a boundary to his praise. The verse opens the psalm's horizon toward the hope of resurrection that later Scripture states plainly (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Philippians 2:10).

The psalm closes on a dynasty that lasts and a name praised forever. No king of Judah fulfilled that; the line of David ended in exile in 586 BC. The closing promise is one reason later readers, Jewish and Christian, looked beyond the first wedding to a king still to come whose name the peoples would praise (Psalm 72:17).

Hope in Isaiah is not optimism about circumstances; it is light given to people who cannot produce it. The people walking in darkness do nothing but see. The light comes from outside, as the reasons in verses 4 to 6 will show: God breaks the yoke, God ends the war, God gives the child.
The guarantee is not the child's lineage or Judah's strength but the zeal of the LORD of Hosts. The hope Isaiah offers rests on God's jealous commitment to finish what he has promised.

The return from exile is pictured as the exodus repeated, with the Euphrates playing the part of the Red Sea. Israel's hope is grounded in what God has already done: the one who made a road through the sea will make a road home. Isaiah develops the highway into the Way of Holiness (35:8) and the highway for God himself (40:3).

Waiting on the LORD is not passive resignation but active expectancy that receives what it cannot produce. The sequence of flying, running, and walking has often been noticed: the promise ends not in soaring but in the ordinary daily walk, where the strength to keep going is most needed.
The picture of hope is bodily and communal: food, drink, dancing, old and young together. Biblical hope does not float free of the earth; it restores the good things of creation to a forgiven people.

God takes the people's despair seriously enough to quote it exactly. Hope in the chapter is not the denial of the lament but God's answer to it: the bones really are dry, and God will raise them anyway.
Hope here is not a feeling the prisoners manufacture but a bond that holds them to God's promise. They are addressed as people who belong to hope while still in captivity.
Seeing God is the goal of human life in the biblical hope (Revelation 22:4; 1 John 3:2). The church later called it the beatific vision, a name taken from this beatitude's promise.
The saying assumes a future with God that is more real than present wealth. Where the treasure is, the heart goes, so hope is shaped by what a person invests in.

Jesus calls death sleep, as Scripture does when it speaks of the dead who will be raised. The laughter of the mourners is the world's verdict that death is final; Jesus' word is the verdict of the one who will overturn it.

The hope of resurrection rests on God's faithfulness to his covenant, not on anything in human nature. Interpreters differ on how the argument works: some see it proving that the patriarchs live now with God, which implies a future bodily resurrection to complete that life; others think Jesus argues directly that God's covenant love must defeat death. Both readings ground the hope in who God is.
Birth pains are pain with a future. Paul uses the same image for the whole creation groaning toward redemption (Romans 8:22).
The parable turns fearful signs into signs of approaching summer. The events that bring suffering also mean that the time of harvest and fulfillment is close.

Each reading has to explain something. The critical view must explain why Mark kept a saying he supposedly knew had failed; the futurist must answer Mark's own use of genea for contemporaries; the preterist and mixed views must account for how closely verse 30 follows verses 24 to 27. The timing is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ; the return itself is confessed by all the creeds.
Christian hope is not calculation but readiness. Not knowing the time is a reason for watchfulness, not for indifference.

The promise draws on the prophets' picture of a banquet of rich food and aged wine for all peoples on God's mountain, when death is swallowed up (Isaiah 25:6-8). The meal before his death is a pledge of the meal after it.

Whichever ending is original, the Gospel ends with the risen Lord still at work. The hope Mark proclaims is not only that Jesus rose once but that he lives and reigns, and that his rising opens a future the church now lives toward.
Simeon's life is defined by what he is waiting for. Luke shows hope as a patient, specific expectation that God will keep his word.
Luke names a whole circle of people waiting for Jerusalem's redemption. Hope in these chapters is a community's shared expectation, kept alive in prayer until God answers it.

The beatitudes place the fulfillment in the future, ‘you will be filled’, ‘you will laugh’, so that present suffering is borne in hope. The reversal is certain because God has promised it, not because the present condition is good.

‘The living one’ is the angels' title for Jesus. The hope the chapter gives is not a comforting memory of a dead teacher but the claim that he is alive, so that seeking him among the dead is simply looking in the wrong place.
The risen Jesus eats. Christian hope is not the escape of souls from bodies but the renewal of bodily life, and the Scriptures' picture of the age to come is a feast (Isaiah 25:6-8, Luke 13:29).
Eternal life in John begins now and has its goal in the age to come. The spring rises ‘to eternal life’, pointing the present gift toward its completion.

The manna sustained life for a day at a time and could not keep the wilderness generation from dying. The bread from heaven gives a life that death does not end, which is why John can speak both of never dying (11:26) and of being raised (6:40).

Calling death sleep is not a denial that Lazarus is dead (verse 14). It names death from the side of the one who can wake the sleeper, which is how the New Testament teaches believers to speak of their dead (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14).

The same words spoken to opponents and to disciples mean different things. For the disciples the separation is temporary, and Jesus will explain in 14:2-3 that he goes to prepare a place and will come back for them.

Eternal life is described as the gift sought by those who look for glory, honor, and immortality from God. The goal of the good life is not self-made virtue but the incorruptible life God gives, which 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 identifies with the resurrection.
Christian hope is not optimism based on circumstances; Abraham's circumstances offered none. It is confidence resting on God's word and God's power, hope ‘upon’ God when every human hope has failed.

The goal of justification is glory: the restoration of what humanity lost (3:23) and the sharing of God's own glory (8:18, 8:30). Christian hope looks to that future, and its certainty is the ground for present rejoicing.
Grace reigns to eternal life. The story that began with death entering the world ends, in Paul's telling, with life that has no end, and grace, not sin, has the last word.
The future ‘we will be’ keeps the believer's resurrection ahead. The Christian lives between a death already shared and a resurrection not yet complete, which is the pattern chapter 8 will develop.
‘Eternal life’ is the end toward which the new life runs. It is already begun in those who are in Christ (verse 22's ‘fruit’) and is completed in the age to come.
Hope does not deny present suffering but sets it on a scale beside future glory. The glory is ‘to be revealed’: it already exists in God's purpose and will be disclosed.
Believers groan not because they lack the Spirit but because they have him: the firstfruits make them long for the full harvest. Hope and groaning belong together in this life.
Christian hope is certain in its object and unseen in its present experience. It is expressed not as anxiety but as patient endurance.
Paul refuses a Christianity that is only useful for this life. If the hope ends at death, the self-denial, persecution, and risk believers accept are simply losses.

Resurrection hope does not make present work pointless; it makes it lasting. Because the body and the world are to be raised and renewed, what is done in the Lord in this life carries into the life to come.
Redemption is already possessed (verse 7) and still awaited (verse 14). The Spirit's presence stands between the two as God's pledge that what he has begun he will finish.
The hope of God's calling is not a wish but a certainty grounded in what God has called his people to. Paul prays that they would see it, since hope is weakened more by forgetting than by doubt.
Hope is described as something objective and secure, kept in heaven, not a feeling that rises and falls. Faith and love are what that secure hope produces in the present.
The hope of glory is anchored in Christ's present indwelling. Christian hope rests not on speculation about the future but on who is already present.
‘Not yet’ is the grammar of Christian hope. The promise stands, and the present disorder is not its denial but its unfinished state.
The promise of rest ‘still stands’. The readers live between promise and arrival, in the same position as Israel in the wilderness, with the promise still open to them.
The rest ‘remains’. Whatever share believers have in it now, its fullness lies ahead, and the letter's later language of a city to come (13:14) belongs with it.
Hope has a ‘full assurance’ that is reached by diligence over time. The verses link assurance to perseverance: confidence grows as the believer keeps going, not apart from it.
Hope is ‘set before’ believers as something objective, like a refuge or a prize, which they seize by fleeing to it. Its security lies not in the one who flees but in the place he flees to.

Christian hope is fastened not in the believer's feelings but in heaven, where Jesus already is. Because he entered ‘on our behalf’ as forerunner, his presence behind the curtain is the pledge that his people will follow.
The better hope is the confidence of drawing near to God, which the law's priests alone had on behalf of others. Through Christ it belongs to all his people (4:16, 10:19-22).
Believers are defined as ‘those who eagerly await Him’. Christian hope is not an abstraction but the expectation of a person who has gone into the sanctuary and will come out again.
Hope is something confessed, spoken aloud in the congregation. Its content is the promise of God, and its security is his faithfulness.

The promise is not simply survival but vocation: the faithful will serve as priests and reign. The hope held out to martyrs is a restored human calling, the priestly rule given to Israel at Sinai and to humanity at creation.
